summary: Shackleton Signal is a coop mission-design game for one to four players. Players build the craft, balance its mass, costs, and power, lift off from the Earth, travel to the Moon, return an orbital survey to Earth, and land a rover in the NASA south polar region. Everything players do has a result. More mass means more fuel needed during transit. A faster transfer requires more fuel to enter lunar orbit. A ridge may prevent Sun or Earth view, requiring a different path, an antenna erection, or a relay deployment. The results are based on the NASA LOLA topography, the Diviner temperature products, and JPL Horizons geometric models. Players analyze light and shade data, transmit their findings, and examine their exploration in a permanent journal.
details:
Shackleton Signal lets one player or a crew of up to four design and operate a connected lunar science mission. The objective is to compare sunlight and shadow, return the evidence to Earth and bring the rover home. The intended audience is students and curious beginners who can learn by changing a design and trying again.

MISSION DESIGN AND ENGINEERING

Players begin with a science objective, fit spacecraft components in a 3D assembly bay and choose the rover battery, communications and portable relays in a cargo manifest. Every option changes mass, cost, power, data volume or steering. The complete wet lander travels as payload through launch and lunar capture. A rehearsal compares three builds under nominal conditions, reduced sunlight or a 10% budget cut.

FLIGHT AND OPERATIONS

The launch integrates thrust, changing mass, gravity and atmospheric drag through two stages. Flight can follow guidance or control pitch, throttle and staging. The achieved parking orbit and remaining upper-stage fuel feed two routes to the Moon. A Lambert solution targets JPL Horizons Moon vectors. Express arrives about 48 simulated hours sooner than Economy, with a greater braking requirement. A manual departure error changes the encounter, and a midcourse correction spends actual remaining upper-stage propellant. The Moon-relative approach sets the perilune and capture speed.

The captured orbit determines observation windows, Earth occultation and solar eclipses. The onboard survey continues through radio blackouts while power, heat and storage constrain operations. The crew votes on a solar-particle alert. Flight can preview a later orbital maneuver, its propellant cost and its effect on future observation and contact windows. Returned reconnaissance opens additional landing areas, so collecting the right observation changes where the mission can explore.

SURFACE EXPLORATION AND EVIDENCE

The lander brakes from the flown lunar orbit and touches down on NASA LOLA elevations. The actual touchdown becomes the rover's base. A 2.56 km square grid preserves 5 m elevation samples across three landing zones and six pads. Rim Overlook opens after South Ridge data reaches Earth and adds its own shadow, sunlight and communications stops.

Route planning compares distance, sunlight, Earth contact and predicted battery use, checking terrain between grid points. The rover can sweep for thirteen map features and select one for a separate radiometer reading. The catalog compares the visible solar disk, tracking-panel output, direct sunlight on a slope and antenna clearance. For example, a panel can see half the Sun while its slope receives zero direct sunlight. At a radio shadow, observations stay onboard until the rover drives into contact, raises a suitable mast or uses a powered portable relay. Two relays can form a terrain-dependent chain.

The final report records the readings actually received on Earth, battery reserve, radio blackouts, route and touchdown. A saved journal lets players revisit discoveries, replay when an observation was acquired and delivered, and compare two expeditions. Contextual instructions, guided flight, F1 explanations and rover practice introduce the controls gradually.

COLLABORATION, SCIENCE AND TOOLS

Flight, Systems, Science and Comms share the mission while each player has their own view and responsibilities. Solo play covers all stations. The game supports online room codes and Direct IP. Automated tests ran all four stations together through the new transfer, orbital survey, landing, blocked-link discovery and eventual downlink on one PC. Cross-network human playtesting remains a development task.

NASA LOLA elevations, Diviner modelled peak temperatures and JPL Horizons geometry directly affect player decisions. The flight model uses planar patched conics, instantaneous departure and correction impulses, spherical gravity and staged polar capture. The survey and surface use a fixed lighting scenario. Vehicle capacities, prices and operating limits are fictional educational settings. Low Diviner temperatures identify candidates for follow-up, and the surface readings compare modelled illumination.

314 studios built the game in Godot 4.7.2 using GDScript, with editable original Blender models. Python, NumPy and Pillow prepare data and materials. A TypeScript service using Cloudflare D1 and WebRTC connects online rooms. OpenAI Codex assisted research, code, data processing, procedural art/audio, modelling and testing. OpenAI ImageGen produced the visibly marked title art. The demo uses captured gameplay with a visible SI-assistance disclosure. Original contributions use Apache 2.0. External datasets and assets retain the credited terms. The public release includes the Windows game, editable source, Blender files, license documentation and a full asset ledger.
